variants.headline: Builder left unpaid for work done
variants.sub: The builder {builder} is owed payment by the client {client} for completed work.
variants.body:
The client {client} has not paid the builder {builder} for work done. The amount owed is {owed}. After three missed months the builder stops work. For {target}, the event raises the basic question of responsibility when a construction undertaking requires payment as well as performance.

A receivable is not cash received. We judge the stewardship of {target} inadequate; practical responsibility should be assessed against a demanding standard.

variants.headline: A construction payment fails to arrive
variants.sub: Payment for work done by {builder} has been missed by {client}.
variants.body:
The builder {builder} is owed {owed} by the client {client} for work already done. The rule is that three missed months bring a stop to work. Readers considering {target} should distinguish the current payment failure from a claim that the stopping point has already been reached.

A receivable is not cash received. We judge the stewardship of {target} inadequate; practical responsibility should be assessed against a demanding standard.

variants.headline: Work delivered, payment outstanding
variants.sub: The client {client} has not paid {builder} for building work done.
variants.body:
Payment for work done by {builder} has been missed by {client}, with {owed} owed. Work stops after three missed months. An assessment of {target} should begin with the present obligation to pay, rather than treat a rule about prolonged non-payment as proof of a stoppage already in effect.

A receivable is not cash received. We judge the stewardship of {target} inadequate; practical responsibility should be assessed against a demanding standard.
